stories.headline: House Republicans block Massie's bid to impeach Defense Secretary Hegseth
stories.summary: The House voted 211-204 on Tuesday to send Rep. Thomas Massie's impeachment resolution against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth to the Judiciary Committee, which halts the effort for now. President Trump welcomed the result. Democrats, who take control of Congress in January, could bring impeachment up again.
stories.why_it_matters: The articles concern how the US entered and is fighting the war with Iran and other military strikes, so the vote is a test of whether Congress will check the Pentagon's use of force. With Democrats taking both chambers in January, the question of Hegseth's future is likely to return.
stories.background: Pete Hegseth has led the Pentagon since 2025, and the US has been at war with Iran in 2026. Rep. Thomas Massie, a Kentucky Republican who lost a Trump-backed primary this year and is retiring, first moved to impeach Hegseth in September. His eight articles accuse Hegseth of starting the Iran war illegally, directing extrajudicial killings and ignoring rules meant to limit civilian deaths. Because the resolution was privileged, the House had to act on it, and Republican leaders chose a procedural vote rather than an up-or-down impeachment vote. Democrats won both chambers in last week's midterm elections and take over in January.

facts.text: The House voted 211-204 on Tuesday to send the impeachment resolution to the Judiciary Committee, which halts the immediate drive but does not stop Democrats from reviving it after January.
Every House Republican except Massie voted to spare Hegseth, CBS News reported.
NPR reported the House had been on course for a floor vote on impeachment Wednesday before Republicans used the procedural vote.
Trump welcomed the outcome and called Hegseth a 'Great American Patriot'.
Rep. Melanie Stansbury (D-N.M.) said she and other lawmakers could not reach the Capitol in time to vote because of a traffic incident and a police escort.
The eight articles accuse Hegseth of illegally starting the war with Iran, directing extrajudicial killings and ignoring laws meant to minimize civilian casualties.
At his first news conference in six months, Hegseth called the impeachment effort a 'farce' and a 'stunt' and said it was about 'policy disagreements'.
A former Hegseth spokesman called on him to resign and said he should be impeached, CNN reported.
Massie first moved to impeach Hegseth over the Iran war in September.

stories.headline: Republicans pick Jim Jordan to lead House GOP and keep John Thune in the Senate
stories.summary: House Republicans on Tuesday chose Rep. Jim Jordan of Ohio over Rep. Steve Scalise to lead them as the minority party in the next Congress. Senate Republicans re-elected John Thune as their leader after rejecting a push by some senators to delay the vote. Both parties are reorganizing after Republicans lost control of both chambers in the midterms.
stories.why_it_matters: These leaders will decide how Republicans respond to a Democratic Congress during the last two years of Trump's term, including on spending deals, investigations and any impeachment efforts.
stories.background: Republicans lost both the House and the Senate in the Nov. 3 midterm elections, and will be in the minority when the new Congress starts in January. House Speaker Mike Johnson said the day after the election that he would not run for minority leader. Jim Jordan, chairman of the House Judiciary Committee, co-founded the hardline Freedom Caucus and is a close Trump ally; he had sought to lead House Republicans twice before. John Thune of South Dakota has led Senate Republicans for the past two years.

facts.text: Jordan defeated Majority Leader Steve Scalise in a secret ballot of Republicans who will serve in the next Congress.

stories.headline: Bernie Sanders says he won't back Chuck Schumer as Senate Democratic leader
stories.summary: Sen. Bernie Sanders said Tuesday he will not support Chuck Schumer to lead Senate Democrats in the new Congress, saying 'the time is now for change.' No one has formally challenged Schumer, though Sen. Chris Van Hollen is considering it. Schumer said he is confident he will become majority leader.
stories.why_it_matters: Whoever leads the new Democratic Senate majority will set its agenda on spending, investigations and Trump's nominees for the next two years.
stories.background: Democrats won control of the Senate in the Nov. 3 midterms, with at least 54 seats according to The Guardian. Chuck Schumer of New York is the current Democratic leader and is seeking to become majority leader. Some progressives, a major union and some newly elected senators want new leadership. Sanders, an independent from Vermont, caucuses with the Democrats and is a leading progressive.

facts.text: Sanders said Tuesday he would not support Schumer, saying 'the time is now for change'.
NBC News reported that Sanders and Sen. Elissa Slotkin called for new leadership but neither proposed an alternative, and that Sen. Chris Van Hollen of Maryland is considering a challenge.

stories.headline: House Oversight report says federal government failed Epstein's victims for decades
stories.summary: The Republican-led House Oversight Committee released a 137-page final report on its 15-month Epstein investigation, faulting the federal government's handling of the case over decades. It urges the Justice Department to reinterview key witnesses and criticizes the Trump administration's release of Epstein records. Democrats, who will run the committee in January, say their inquiry is just starting.
stories.why_it_matters: The report puts on the record that survivors say federal investigators never questioned them, and it sets up further investigations, including of banks, once Democrats take over committees in January.
stories.background: Jeffrey Epstein was a convicted sex offender whose associates included many powerful people. Public pressure to release government files on him led Congress to pass, and President Trump to sign, the Epstein Files Transparency Act nearly a year ago. The House Oversight Committee, chaired by Rep. James Comer (R-Ky.), interviewed many of Epstein's associates. In September Comer introduced a bill aimed at tactics used to silence victims, saying the government had failed them.

facts.text: The committee released a 137-page report nearly a year after the Epstein Files Transparency Act became law.
The report followed a 15-month investigation and faulted the federal government for decades of failing to hold Epstein accountable.
Chairman James Comer said the federal government 'has failed the survivors' of Epstein's and Ghislaine Maxwell's crimes for decades.
The report says many survivors and other witnesses told the committee they were never approached or properly questioned by federal authorities.
The committee called on the Justice Department to reinterview key witnesses.
The report criticizes the Trump administration over its release of Epstein records, the AP reported.
Democrats said the inquiry is 'just getting started' and plan to examine banks tied to Epstein once they hold majorities in January.
A Politico poll found more voters want Democrats to pursue an affordability agenda than to keep investigating Epstein.
In September, Comer unveiled legislation he said would close human-trafficking loopholes exposed by the Epstein case.

stories.headline: Kennedy family members ask court to block Trump's arch near Arlington Cemetery
stories.summary: Nine members of the Kennedy family asked a federal judge in Washington to block construction of President Trump's planned 250-foot arch near Arlington National Cemetery. They argue it would cast a shadow over family graves and disrupt the view from John F. Kennedy's eternal flame. The filing joins an existing lawsuit as Trump visits the cemetery for Veterans Day.
stories.why_it_matters: The case is one of several testing whether the president can build a large monument on federal land near a national cemetery without approval from Congress or full environmental review.
stories.background: President Trump has proposed a roughly 250-foot triumphal arch in the Washington area, near Arlington National Cemetery, where President John F. Kennedy and other Kennedy family members are buried. Earlier this year, Vietnam War veterans and an architectural historian sued to stop it, saying Congress had not approved it. Arlington County, Virginia, also sued, arguing the administration skipped required environmental reviews. The Kennedy relatives are asking to join one of these existing cases.

facts.text: Nine Kennedy family members asked a judge to block the 250-foot arch.
The request was filed Monday in the US District Court for the District of Columbia and joins an existing lawsuit.

stories.headline: Democrats lead narrowly as Mississippi and Alaska Senate counts near the end
stories.summary: Ballot deadlines passed Tuesday in Mississippi, where Democrat Scott Colom holds a narrow lead over Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith. In Alaska, Democrat Mary Peltola's lead over Sen. Dan Sullivan grew to about 2,500 votes, and a judge is weighing a lawsuit from her campaign over absentee ballots. They are the last two Senate races not yet called.
stories.why_it_matters: The two races will decide how large the new Democratic Senate majority is, which affects how easily it can pass bills and confirm or block nominees.
stories.background: Democrats won control of the Senate in the Nov. 3 midterms, but races in Mississippi and Alaska remain too close to call. Mississippi rarely has close statewide races, and a large number of absentee and provisional ballots is still being processed. In Alaska, counting of absentee ballots continues; earlier this month a federal judge dismissed a Justice Department lawsuit that sought to delay certification of the state's Senate race and separate certain ballots.

facts.text: Tuesday was the deadline in Mississippi for provisional ballots to be resolved and for mail-in absentee ballots to arrive, and Colom extended his lead.

stories.headline: California voters reject one-time tax on billionaires' wealth
stories.summary: California voters rejected Proposition 40, which would have imposed a one-time 5% tax on the wealth of residents worth more than $1 billion. The measure split Democrats and drew record opposition spending, much of it from the tech industry. Supporters had seen it as a model for wealth taxes elsewhere.
stories.why_it_matters: The result shows that even in a strongly Democratic year and state, voters turned down a direct tax on the very rich, which is likely to shape whether other states or Congress try similar taxes.
stories.background: A wealth tax charges people on the value of what they own, such as company shares, rather than only on income. Prop 40 would have charged billionaires 5% once, on most of their wealth. Major tech figures funded a large campaign against it, while some Democrats and progressives backed it. The vote took place in the Nov. 3 election, in which Democrats won control of Congress.

facts.text: Prop 40 would have imposed a one-time 5% tax on the wealth of Californians with a net worth above $1 billion, including company shares.
